implementation_notes: The standard library is the pattern: mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b) exchanges two values in place without deinitialising either one, allocates nothing and cannot fail - Rust has no exceptions, and the swap runs no user code, so there is no guarantee to declare and no ADL protocol to provide. For a type that keeps its representation in one field, the exchange is `std::mem::swap(&mut self.state, &mut other.state)`; when a value must be moved out first, mem::replace(dest, src) returns the old value (mem::take when a Default placeholder is acceptable), which is the idiomatic "stage the new state, then install it", and Box/Arc pointers are exchanged in O(1). The unsafe ptr::swap/ptr::swap_nonoverlapping forms are the raw-pointer versions used inside collections, where the aliasing and pinning rules are the caller's responsibility.
pitfalls: mem::swap needs two distinct &mut references, so `mem::swap(&mut x, &mut x)` does not compile; the raw-pointer forms (ptr::swap) are undefined behaviour if the pointers overlap or were derived from the same &mut.

Once a value is pinned, exchanging its contents (for example through Pin::get_unchecked_mut) breaks the pinning guarantee for self-referential types; swap the boxed handle (Pin<Box<T>>) instead of the pinned contents.
mem::swap is not atomic: for state shared between threads use AtomicPtr, ArcSwap or a Mutex rather than exchanging fields.

mem::take silently installs a Default value and mem::replace runs no destructor inside the call, so an expensive Default impl makes the exchange expensive and ignoring the returned old value keeps the previous state alive.
